opus-5.5.text:
That's a really good question, and honestly it's something I've had to come to terms with over time. I'm naturally pretty introverted. If you leave me alone, I'd happily sit in front of my computer and write code for twelve hours straight, and that actually recharges me. Talking with people, especially in a meeting or a long discussion, takes a lot of energy out of me. After a day of conversations I often just want to be quiet for a while.

But I've realized that those conversations are where a lot of the real value comes from. When you work alone, it's very easy to fall in love with your own ideas. You think something is elegant or important, but you're living inside your own head. The moment you explain it to someone else, you immediately find out which parts are actually clear and which parts only made sense to you. Sometimes a single question from another person, something like "why would anyone need this?", saves me weeks or even months of going in the wrong direction.

With Taichi especially, I learned that building something technically good is only half the story. If you want people to actually use it, you have to understand what they're struggling with, and you can't get that by staring at your code. Users, collaborators, people from completely different fields, they see problems I would never have imagined.

So the way I think about it now is almost like an investment. The conversation costs me energy in the moment, but it gives me information I can't get any other way. I try to be deliberate about it: have fewer but deeper conversations, prepare well, and then protect enough quiet time afterward to actually digest what I heard and turn it into work. That balance, rather than avoiding people or forcing myself to be someone I'm not, is what's worked best for me.

r001.rationale: The response says that working alone can make someone fall in love with their own ideas and go in the wrong direction, while others’ questions help clarify what is worth pursuing.

r002.rationale: It says conversations with users and collaborators reveal problems they face that Hu would not have imagined, which can guide what Taichi should address.

r003.rationale: Hu says writing code recharges him, in contrast to conversations that take energy out of him.

fable-5.1.text:
You're right that I find it draining. I'm fairly introverted, and after a long day of conversations I feel like my battery is at zero. But I've come to see those conversations as one of the highest-leverage things I can do, so I treat the cost as something worth paying rather than something to avoid.

The main reason is that when you build something for a long time, like I did with Taichi, you develop blind spots. You know every corner of the system, and that makes it almost impossible to see it the way a newcomer does. A user who struggles with your installation process for twenty minutes will tell you something you could never learn by staring at your own code. And you don't need many of those conversations. Two or three honest ones can change your roadmap more than months of internal debate.

There's also something about explaining your work out loud that sharpens your own thinking. When I describe a design decision to someone and I hear myself stumble, that usually means the decision wasn't fully reasoned. The listener doesn't even need to push back. Just having to make it coherent for another person exposes the weak parts.

And then there's the people side, which I underestimated for years. Open source, startups, research, all of it runs on trust. People contribute to your project or join your team because they talked to you and felt something real. You can't replicate that with a well-written README.

So what I've learned is not to avoid these conversations but to be deliberate about them. I batch them when I can, I protect quiet time to recover and actually build, and I try to go into each one with a specific question I want answered. That way the energy I spend comes back as something concrete, instead of just leaving me tired.

r001.rationale: The response describes blind spots from building a system for a long time, but does not say that prolonged isolation leaves a researcher unable to identify what to work on.

r002.rationale: It says conversations with users reveal problems they encounter, such as installation difficulties, and that this feedback can change the roadmap.

r003.rationale: The response says Hu protects quiet time to recover and build, but does not state that writing code restores the energy he spends on social interaction.

astra-6.text: I find those conversations draining, but I still think they’re valuable. When I’m working on something, a lot of the context is just in my head. Explaining it to someone else forces me to make that context explicit, and sometimes I realize I don’t understand a part of it as clearly as I thought. Other people also ask questions I wouldn’t ask myself. So there’s a real benefit, even if I need some quiet time afterward. For me, the challenge is finding a balance between getting that outside perspective and having enough uninterrupted time to do the work.

r001.rationale: The response says explaining work and hearing questions can clarify understanding, but does not say prolonged isolation prevents a researcher from identifying what to work on.

r002.rationale: It describes gaining outside perspective, but does not identify communication as a way to find unsolved problems that one’s technology could address.

r003.rationale: The response mentions needing quiet time after conversations; it does not say Yuanming Hu restores his energy by writing code.

Then someone asks a simple question, and I realize there’s something I haven’t thought through. So even though talking can be draining for me, it can also help me clarify my thinking.
